slides.narration: Chapter 18: The Intra-Generation Split. Why is the bottom quark heavier than the tau lepton? The answer comes from the most fundamental equation in Maya math — and from Einstein's E equals mc squared.

The Fibonacci identity — phi squared equals phi plus one — is not just algebra. It is an energy budget. The quark's total budget is phi squared. This budget splits between mass and force. What goes to force — measured by the strong coupling alpha-s — cannot also be mass.

The quark mass equals the lepton mass times phi squared minus the strong coupling. The strong coupling depends on the quark's own mass — creating a self-referential loop whose fixed point is the physical mass. For the bottom quark: 4.28 GeV, matching the measurement to 2.3 percent.

lines: When α_s > φ: quarks become lighter
slides.narration: The formula makes a prediction: when the strong coupling exceeds phi — the golden ratio itself — the quark becomes lighter than its lepton partner. This is exactly what happens with the strange quark and the muon. The reversal threshold is the golden ratio.
